section_summary: This section contains articles and background reports on Japan’s automobile industry, followed by U.S. diplomatic correspondence about restrictions on Ford and General Motors under Japan’s Automobile Industry Control Law. State Department memoranda debate whether those restrictions violate the 1911 U.S.–Japan treaty and whether further protest would be useful. The section ends during a longer policy memorandum that continues beyond page 287.

subfiles.title: Automobile Industry in Japan Growing Gradually
subfiles.about: A newspaper writer surveys Japanese automobile production, prices, history and government support.
subfiles.summary: The article describes growing domestic production of trucks and small cars, while American makes still dominate Japanese roads. It links government support for local manufacturers to the military value of motor vehicles and predicts cheaper cars for the public.

subfiles.title: Partial List of Previous Reports on Automobile Industry in Japan
subfiles.about: Lists eight earlier reports and despatches on Japanese automobile manufacturing.
subfiles.summary: Indexes earlier reports on Nissan, Datsun, Ford’s Yokohama plant and the proposed control law.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversations with Mr. Benjamin Kopf
subfiles.about: Notes that Kopf’s views on Japan’s automobile industry have appeared in earlier reports.
subfiles.summary: The writer says earlier State Department communications accurately conveyed Kopf’s views.

subfiles.title: Automobile Industry, Japan-Manchoukuo Year Book, 1936
subfiles.about: Reviews motor vehicle use, production, manufacturers and proposed government control of Japan’s automobile industry.
subfiles.summary: The extract traces growth in taxis, buses and trucks and gives figures for domestic production, imports, parts and vehicles in use. It describes leading Japanese makers and the extensive role of Ford and General Motors. Its final pages outline the proposed licensing law, Japanese ownership requirements and warnings issued to the two foreign firms.

subfiles.title: Japanese Automobile Industry Control Law
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports Ford’s complaint that officials barred plant improvements beyond the express terms of the control law.
subfiles.summary: Boyce relays Benjamin Kopf’s account that Japanese officials refused permission for a foundry and larger machine department at Ford’s Yokohama plant, although Kopf said the changes would improve efficiency without increasing output.

subfiles.title: Instruction on Ford’s Yokohama Plant and the Control Law
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requests monitoring and Embassy comment on Ford’s allegation of discriminatory enforcement.
subfiles.summary: Directs the Embassy to track adverse developments and assess whether U.S. action is warranted.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Treaty Principles in the Automobile Control Dispute
subfiles.about: Explains why the Department stopped short of pursuing its treaty argument with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recounts competing readings of Articles I and VII of the 1911 treaty. Doubts about the rights of U.S. corporations and nonresident individuals led the Department to withhold a draft telegram and avoid further debate.

subfiles.title: Application of the Automobile Industry Control Law—Position of the Ford Motor Company
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards Ford’s account of restrictions and asks whether renewed representations to Japan are appropriate.
subfiles.summary: Grew reviews the control law, Japan’s treaty interpretation and Ford’s inability to obtain permission for a new plant and related operations. He explains Ford’s commercial reasons for expansion but doubts that diplomatic protest would alter the Japanese military’s determination to develop a domestic industry. He refers Ford’s requests for protest and informal inquiry to the Department.

subfiles.title: Statement Regarding Ford’s Attempt to Extend Its Assembly Plant in Japan
subfiles.from: B. Kopf, Ford Motor Company of Japan Ltd.
subfiles.about: Details Ford’s unsuccessful attempts to expand its Yokohama facilities.
subfiles.summary: Kopf describes opposition to land purchases, unanswered factory applications, refusal of dock and dredging permits, and restrictions on manufacturing and machining. He reports fixed Ford and General Motors production quotas and pressure on transport operators to buy Japanese vehicles.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Ford’s Request for Renewed Treaty Representations
subfiles.about: Recommends against further representations over Ford’s factory plans.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews earlier treaty discussions and the unused draft instruction challenging Japan’s position. It concurs with the Embassy that further argument is unlikely to change Japan’s policy and appends an instruction declining to raise the matter again.

subfiles.title: Telegram on the Automobile Industry Control Law
subfiles.about: Responds to the Embassy’s despatch on Ford and the control law.
subfiles.summary: The Department declines renewed representations and asks the Embassy to explain its position to Ford.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary Division of Far Eastern Affairs Note
subfiles.about: An almost illegible note survives with a February 1936 date.
subfiles.summary: Only the division heading and a partial date are legible.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Mr. Hamilton on the Japanese Treaty Contention
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan’s proposed automobile law would violate Article I of the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.summary: Ward rejects the Japanese Foreign Office’s distinction between individuals and corporations. He argues that American citizens must be able to use Japanese corporations to manufacture on equal terms with Japanese subjects and recommends a firm statement that the proposed law would breach the treaty.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser’s Memorandum on Corporate Rights under the 1911 Treaty
subfiles.about: Supports Ward’s treaty analysis using a California court decision.
subfiles.summary: The Legal Adviser argues that denying Americans the ability to form corporations would undermine Article I’s trade guarantees. The memorandum discusses K. Tashiro et al. v. Jordan and distinguishes rights of locally formed corporations from those of foreign corporations under Article VII.

subfiles.title: Policy with Regard to Proposed Automobile Legislation in Japan
subfiles.about: Examines proposed automobile legislation, treaty rights, affected American interests and possible U.S. policy.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reproduces Japan’s 1935 notice to General Motors, an outline of the proposed law and a newspaper account of its provisions. It analyzes Articles I and VII of the 1911 treaty, including whether American individuals, U.S. corporations and American owned Japanese corporations have different rights. It estimates the significance of the Japanese market for Ford and General Motors and argues for continued U.S. protest despite practical and legal risks. The memorandum continues beyond page 287.
